title: To Kill a Mockingbird
synopsis: Maycomb, Alabama, summer. You are Scout. Your father, Atticus, will be defending a Black man no Maycomb jury wants acquitted. Don't shoot a mockingbird.

nodes.text: Maycomb in August moves slow because it is too hot to move any other way. Men's collars wilt by nine in the morning. You have gone barefoot since June and the soles of your feet are hard enough for gravel now. Dill turns up from Meridian, small for seven, with a whole vocabulary of lies about his father. Jem counts the seconds out loud while you roll down Miss Rachel's hill inside a tire.

choices.consequence: The count comes to nineteen. You come out of the tire at the bottom sick and delighted, with a scraped elbow, and you demand another go immediately.
You sit on the porch steps and watch nothing happen for an hour, and learn the exact order in which the neighbours' screen doors bang shut before supper.

nodes.text: The house three doors down keeps its shutters closed in daylight and its yard gone over to Johnson grass. Nobody has laid eyes on the Radley boy since the afternoon he put a pair of scissors through his father's leg, and that was before you were born. Dill dares Jem to run up and touch the porch. Jem thinks about it for three days, which is how you know he is scared.

choices.consequence: Jem runs up, slaps the wood, and runs back, and not one of you looks behind. A shutter moves. Later there is chewing gum in the knothole of the oak.

You stand at the gate and count to a hundred and go home for supper before dark. You dream about that house anyway, every night that week. You stay on the sidewalk. The decision moves you toward Calpurnia and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: She has run this kitchen since before your mother died and she gets you by the collar for being rude to a guest at your own table, and she is right to. Her hand is wide and hard as a bed slat. She teaches you cursive out of spite when you are bored. At her church she talks a different way, and you learn that some ways of speaking are just for staying safe in.

choices.consequence: You apologise to Walter Cunningham for hollering about the syrup, and you mean about half of it, and Calpurnia accepts the half without comment.
You say he is nothing but a Cunningham and she takes you into the kitchen and shuts the door, and you never tell anybody what she said in there.

nodes.text: Miss Caroline is from up in north Alabama and wears a red-striped dress and is twenty-one years old. She finds out you can already read, decides your father has taught you wrong, and tells you to quit. Then she offers Walter Cunningham a quarter for lunch, not knowing a Cunningham never takes what he cannot pay back. You explain this out loud to the room and get your hand switched for it.

choices.consequence: You promise to stop reading, then read on the front porch where she cannot possibly see you, which is the arrangement your father quietly proposes.

You stand in the corner with your nose to the plaster and conclude that school is a thing done to a person rather than for one. You argue. The decision moves you toward Atticus and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: He is nearly fifty, wears glasses, and cannot play football for the Methodists, which is a genuine grievance. Evenings he reads with his legs crossed and lets you climb on him like furniture. When you announce you are not going back to school he does not argue. He says you never really know a man until you get down inside his skin and walk around in it. Then he goes back to his paper.

choices.consequence: You try it on Miss Caroline: first day in a strange county, twenty-six children who all know things she does not. It almost works, and it startles you.
You say people are just what they are, and he says all right, and lets it lie there, and you keep turning it over for a whole year afterward.

nodes.text: Tom Robinson is twenty-five. He is married to Helen, has three children, and has picked cotton for Link Deas since he was a boy. His left arm caught in a cotton gin when he was twelve and it hangs a foot shorter than the other and does not work. He is accused of raping Mayella Ewell. The judge hands the case to your father, and your father does not do what most Maycomb lawyers would.

choices.consequence: Atticus says he could not hold his head up in town, or tell you and Jem anything ever again, if he let it go. You repeat this at school and get in a fight.
Cecil Jacobs announces in the schoolyard that your daddy defends Negroes, and the word he actually uses lands like a thrown rock. You ask what it means. Atticus tells you.

nodes.text: Your father takes an extension cord, a light bulb, and a book down to the jail and sits in a kitchen chair by the door. Four cars come in from the Old Sarum road with their headlights switched off. You and Jem and Dill are in the doorway of the Jitney Jungle across the street. Jem will not go home when he is told to, and the look on Atticus's face is not anger.

choices.consequence: You ask Mr. Cunningham about his entailment and his boy Walter and say to tell him hey. He crouches down, says he will, and takes the whole lot of them home.
You stay in the shadow and watch your father sit alone between a locked door and twenty men. Jem breaks first and runs out, and the night tips over from there.

nodes.text: The whole county comes in on wagons and eats dinner on the courthouse lawn. By the time the three of you slip inside, the floor is packed to the walls. Reverend Sykes takes you upstairs to the balcony where the colored folks sit, and four men give up their front-row seats without anybody asking them to. From up there you can see the top of your father's head and Tom Robinson's shoulders.

choices.consequence: You take a borrowed seat among people who stood so a white child could see, and it will be some years before you understand what that cost them.

You get as far as the lawn and cannot hear a word of it, and Jem says he is not missing this for anything, so back up the stairs you go. You sit on the lawn. The decision moves you toward Cross-Examination and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Mayella is nineteen, has washed her face for court, and is the only person in that room more frightened than the defendant. Atticus calls her ma'am and Miss Mayella and she accuses him of mocking her, because nobody has ever been polite to her before. He asks about the seven children she raises alone, and whether her father is easy to live with when he has been drinking. She quits answering.

choices.consequence: You watch the jury look at her hands and then at her father's, and you watch Atticus ask her to be brave one time, and you watch her refuse.

You want to cry for her and cannot square that with what she is doing to Tom Robinson, and both things stay true in you at the same time. You cry. The decision moves you toward Tom's Testimony and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: He puts his good hand on the Bible and the left one slides off it, and the whole courtroom sees the arm. He says he passed that gate most evenings and did chores for her free, for nothing, because there was nobody else on that place to do them. Mr. Gilmer asks him why. He says he felt right sorry for her. In this county a Black man has just said he pitied a white woman.

choices.consequence: You watch the jury's faces close one after another, like shutters going down a street, and you understand you have just heard the case lost out loud.

Dill starts crying so hard you have to walk him outside, and on the steps he says it was the way that man talked to him, like he was dirt. You choose to hold breath. It opens the route to Closing, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Atticus does something you have never seen him do. He unbuttons his vest, unbuttons his collar, loosens his tie, and takes off his coat in public. He tells the jury the state has produced no medical evidence and one witness whose account has been contradicted. He says a court is the one place a poor man stands equal to a rich one. Then he says a court is only as sound as its jury.

choices.consequence: Reverend Sykes leans across and tells you to stand up. Your father is passing below. Every person in the balcony is already on their feet for him.
You sit still and count the ceiling fans while the jury files out, and Reverend Sykes says he has never once seen a jury decide for a Black man.

nodes.text: The jury stays out longer than anybody expects, hours instead of minutes, which people will later say must have meant something. When they file back in, not one of them looks at the defendant. The clerk reads it down the line: guilty, guilty, guilty, guilty. Jem's hands are locked on the balcony rail and his shoulders are shaking, and he keeps saying it is not right, quietly, over and over.

choices.consequence: You hold it in because Jem is not holding it in and one of you has to. On the walk home in the dark neither of you says a single word. You choose to don't cry in the balcony. It opens the route to Aunt Alexandra, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You cry with your face in Reverend Sykes's coat sleeve and he lets you, and down below your father packs his briefcase alone and walks out up the aisle.

nodes.text: Aunt Alexandra has moved into the house for the good of the family, and she believes in Fine Folks and in what people will say. The missionary circle meets in your parlour to discuss the poor Mrunas in Africa, and then, over the charlotte, complains about how sulky the help has been since the trial. Your aunt hears every word of it, and pours the coffee, and corrects nobody.

choices.consequence: You wear your britches under the dress and hand the cookies round without spilling one. Miss Maudie catches your eye across the room and says nothing at all.

You put on the pink dress and the shoes and try being a lady, and it feels exactly like standing still for a photograph that takes an hour. You concede. The decision moves you toward Tom Tries to Run and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Your father meant to appeal and thought there was a real chance in it. Tom did not wait. During exercise at Enfield Prison Farm he went over the fence in full daylight with one working arm, and the guards fired seventeen times. Helen Robinson is on her porch with the three children when Atticus drives out to tell her, and she goes down in the yard before he reaches the step.

choices.consequence: You think about a man who could not climb with one arm climbing anyway, and about how many of those seventeen shots anybody actually needed.
The newspaper calls it typical of his kind. The town shakes its head for two days and then talks about the county fair. You keep hold of that for years.

nodes.text: The county pageant needs a ham. Mrs. Crenshaw builds one out of chicken wire and cured brown cloth, and once you are inside it your arms are pinned and you can only see out through a slit. You miss your cue asleep behind the stage and come on during the finale, and the whole auditorium laughs. Jem waits at the back so you do not have to walk out past everybody.

choices.consequence: You keep the ham on for the walk home, because taking it off means facing Judge Taylor's wife, and the wire creaks with every single step you take.
You try to get out of it and cannot work the fastenings alone, and Jem says leave it, it is dark, there is nobody left out there to see you.

nodes.text: No moon, no streetlight on that stretch, and the big schoolyard oak throwing everything under it black. You hear feet behind you and stop walking; the feet stop too. Jem says it is Cecil trying to scare you again. You go on, and they come on faster, and they are not a child's feet. Then something takes hold of the chicken wire around your middle and your arms will not come free.

choices.consequence: You try to run and the costume takes your legs out from under you, and you go down in the dirt while two men fight over the top of you. You choose to run. It opens the route to Saved, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You stand still inside the wire and hear your brother scream once, and then a sound like a green stick breaking, and then somebody breathing very hard.

nodes.text: There is a fourth person under that tree and you never see him arrive. Somebody grabs, somebody grunts, and then a man is carrying Jem toward the road with his head hanging back, and you run after the shape of them. Aunt Alexandra is at the door. Dr. Reynolds comes in his shirtsleeves. Sheriff Tate goes back out to the oak with a flashlight and stays out there a long while.

choices.consequence: You stand in the doorway while the doctor sets the arm, and Jem sleeps through all of it and does not yet know that anything has happened to him.

You go looking for whoever carried him and find a man in the corner behind the door, and you do not look straight at him, not yet. You find the man. The decision moves you toward Behind the Door and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: He is against the wall in the corner of Jem's room, the exact spot the open door would hide. His skin is white the way things kept out of the sun go white. His hair is thin and dead-looking, his cheeks are hollow, and his hands are small. When Dr. Reynolds turns the lamp up he flinches from it. He looks at Jem asleep, then at you, and his mouth does something like a smile.

choices.consequence: You say hey, Boo, before you have decided to say anything. Aunt Alexandra's hand goes to her mouth. He looks down at the floor, pleased. You commit to smile. By The Porch, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You look at him the way children look, straight on and all the way, and he takes it without minding, and afterward you are ashamed of yourself.

nodes.text: Sheriff Tate says Bob Ewell fell on his own knife and will not be argued out of it, and your father finally works out who is being protected. Boo whispers that he would like to say good night to Jem, and touches his hair once, and then you take his arm the way a lady does at a wedding and walk him up the street to his own door. He goes inside. You never see him again.

choices.consequence: You turn round on his porch and look at the street from his side of it: your house, the oak, four seasons of children going by. You see all of it.

You stand a moment and go, because it is late and Jem's arm is broken, and the street watches you the whole way back down to your own gate. You look briefly. The decision moves you toward Atticus, Tucking In and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: He has been reading in Jem's room since ten, in the same chair, glasses pushed up on his forehead. He finishes the book you asked for, the one about a boy everybody is sure did it who turns out not to have. You are three-quarters asleep and you tell him so. He carries you across the hall, and then goes back in, and he is still in that chair when the light comes.

choices.consequence: You go under before he reaches the bed and never hear what he says in the doorway, and it does not matter, because you know it already. You choose to sleep. It opens the route to Years On, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You keep your eyes shut and hear him settle back into Jem's chair for the whole night, and that is the last thing that year has to teach you.

nodes.text: Jem's arm healed short at the elbow and he never minded it. Aunt Alexandra stayed on. Calpurnia's kitchen belongs to somebody else now. The county built a new school out on the highway with a gymnasium and a lunchroom, and the courthouse smells the same as it always did, and Helen Robinson still walks the long way round past the Ewell place out of habit that nobody has ever asked her about.

choices.consequence: You keep the house on the street where you learned everything, and find you cannot stop turning it over, and one winter you begin setting it down on paper.
You go to law school because your father made it look like a job an ordinary person could do, and it proves to be a very different job than that.

You come back after college and take the schoolroom instead of the courtroom, and every year some child asks you about the Radley place. You take the third path. The decision moves you toward Porch and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You write it years later from a long way off, a small book about a town you loved and could not forgive. In go the tire and the gum in the knothole and the balcony standing up. People read it in schools and stop you in airports to say it changed them. Helen Robinson's children are grown and gone by then, one of them a nurse in Mobile. Nobody ever asks you about them.

You take the bar, and then, when he can no longer manage the stairs, you take his office above the drugstore. Same rolltop desk, same smell of it. You lose cases he would have lost and one or two he would not have. Nobody warned you how much of this work is sitting on somebody's porch afterward with your hat in your hands, and how little of that part is law.

You come home to teach and you stay. Your students' grandparents sat on that jury; a few of your students have their eyes. Some evenings you walk up to the Radley place, which belongs to nobody now, and sit on the boards and look down the street the way he did. The town changes at the speed towns change, which is to say by funerals. You are patient about it. Somebody taught you how.
